title: AI-Assisted Colonoscopy Shows Promise for Lynch Syndrome but Falls Short of Breakthrough
excerpt: The largest randomized trial of artificial intelligence in Lynch syndrome colonoscopy found that current AI tools do not significantly improve detection rates when used by expert endoscopists, though they show potential for spotting hard-to-see flat lesions.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The CADLY2 trial involved 757 patients across 9 centers, showing no significant AI detection improvement.
  • Lynch syndrome carriers have adenoma miss rates over 48%, double that of the general population.
  • Current AI tools may need specific training for Lynch syndrome's unique flat lesions to improve detection.
  • Earlier trials indicated AI could enhance detection of hard-to-spot flat adenomas in Lynch syndrome patients.
  • Identifying Lynch syndrome early can prevent 30 to 45 colorectal cancers per 100 carriers over a lifetime.

  • CADLY2, the largest randomized trial of AI in Lynch syndrome colonoscopy (757 patients, 9 centers, 4 countries), found no significant improvement in adenoma detection: 33.8% with AI vs. 30.9% without (p = 0.409).
  • An earlier pilot trial did find AI significantly improved detection of flat adenomas — the hardest-to-spot lesions and a hallmark of Lynch syndrome pathology.
  • Lynch syndrome carriers have adenoma miss rates exceeding 48%, roughly double the rate seen in the general population, making improved detection tools a clinical priority.
  • Researchers say current AI systems trained on common polyps may need Lynch-specific algorithms to address the unique flat, pale lesions characteristic of the syndrome.

Artificial intelligence can be safely integrated into colonoscopy surveillance for Lynch syndrome patients, but current AI tools do not dramatically improve cancer-precursor detection when used by expert endoscopists — a finding that complicates hopes for a technological shortcut against the most common hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome.

That is the central conclusion emerging from two randomized controlled trials and a comprehensive review published in the International Journal of Cancer by Robert Hüneburg and colleagues at the University Hospital Bonn, which houses Germany's National Center for Hereditary Tumor Syndromes.

The CADLY2 Trial

The CADLY2 trial, presented as a late-breaking abstract at ESGE Days 2026 in Milan, is the largest randomized study evaluating AI in Lynch syndrome colonoscopy to date. It randomized 757 individuals with Lynch syndrome across 9 expert centers in 4 countries, with 733 included in the final analysis. Thirty-seven experienced endoscopists participated.

The primary endpoint was clear: AI-assisted colonoscopy using computer-aided detection (CADe) did not significantly improve adenoma detection compared with standard high-definition white-light colonoscopy. The adenoma detection rate was 33.8 percent with CADe versus 30.9 percent without (adjusted odds ratio 1.14; 95% CI 0.83–1.57; p = 0.409). Secondary detection outcomes were consistent with the primary result.

Why Lynch Syndrome Is Different

Lynch syndrome carriers face a lifetime colorectal cancer risk of up to 70 percent. Even with colonoscopy surveillance every one to two years from early adulthood, interval cancers remain common. The reason lies in the biology: Lynch syndrome lesions are characteristically flat, pale, small, and fast-growing. Across six back-to-back colonoscopy studies, adenoma miss rates consistently exceeded 48 percent — approximately double the rate seen in average-risk populations.

Most current AI systems were trained primarily on sporadic, polypoid adenomas — the raised, grape-like growths common in general screening populations. The subtle, flat lesions of Lynch syndrome fall outside their training distribution.

"Small and flat adenomas in particular are at risk of being overlooked even by experienced gastroenterologists."

— Prof. Jacob Nattermann, University Hospital Bonn

Signs of Promise

The earlier CADLY pilot trial, involving 96 Lynch syndrome carriers, offered a more encouraging signal. While the overall adenoma detection rate difference was not statistically significant (36% with AI vs. 26.1% without), flat adenomas accounted for 56.6 percent of all adenomas detected with AI assistance, compared to just 20 percent with standard inspection (p = 0.018). This suggested that AI could enhance visualization of the very lesion type most likely to be missed.

The larger TIMELY trial, using a different AI system (Medtronic GI-Genius) in 430 Lynch carriers, found no overall detection improvement but did show a significant increase in the detection of 5–9 mm sessile serrated lesions with AI.

The Path Forward

Hüneburg's review concludes that the current generation of AI tools — designed for average-risk screening populations — may require Lynch-specific algorithmic training to meaningfully improve outcomes. The flat, pale morphology of Lynch syndrome precursors diverges fundamentally from the polypoid adenomas that dominate existing AI training datasets.

In the general screening population, more than 40 randomized trials have consistently shown AI improves adenoma detection rates by 15 to 25 percent. Whether that translates into reduced cancer incidence for Lynch carriers depends on developing systems tuned to their unique biology.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention classifies Lynch syndrome as a Tier 1 genomic condition, meaning evidence-based interventions can substantially reduce related morbidity and mortality. Population-based analyses estimate that identifying Lynch syndrome in early adulthood and initiating guideline-based surveillance prevents approximately 30 to 45 colorectal cancers per 100 carriers over a lifetime.

For the estimated 1 in 279 people worldwide who carry Lynch syndrome — many undiagnosed — the technology is moving in the right direction, if not yet fast enough.
